claims.text: The proposed framework combines high-resolution microstructural descriptors with a machine-learning surrogate model.

A surrogate model such as bagged support vector regression can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior in HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than established finite-element and first-principles approaches.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15%.
The proposed model will be approximately ten times more computationally efficient than conventional simulations.
As-produced HfNbTiVAl10 possesses an intrinsic hierarchical heterostructure characterized by XRD, SEM, and TEM.
The relevant HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure contains intragranular nanoprecipitates and spatially distributed phases and phase boundaries.
The nanoprecipitate distribution and phase boundaries mediate dislocation storage.
The nanoprecipitate distribution and phase boundaries mediate crack arrest.
Using precipitate density, interface characteristics, and other heterogeneity descriptors as model inputs can refine correlations between local structure and macroscopic mechanical response.
Use of a trained surrogate reduces the need for exhaustive first-principles calculations.
Direct DFT or first-principles evaluation of alloy yield and fracture properties is computationally challenging or beyond the reach of common implementations.
Conventional finite-element, DFT, and direct first-principles simulations have larger predictive uncertainties than the proposed model for the same HfNbTiVAl10 properties.
The model is intended to operate under tensile and fracture testing at room temperature and selected elevated temperatures.
The phase and microstructural evolution of HfNbTiVAl10 at the selected elevated temperatures is consistent with prior reports.
Prediction accuracy may fail if characterization does not adequately capture microstructural heterogeneity.
Extrinsic defects or processing anomalies absent from the training data may cause the model to fail.
Prediction performance may deteriorate when extrapolating to temperatures or strain rates not adequately represented in training.
Failure to achieve both at least a 15% accuracy improvement and a tenfold computation-time reduction relative to conventional methods will falsify the hypothesis.
